title: I built 20 reusable skills to make AI coding agents better at actual game development (3D, animation, VFX, debugging) Copy title
author: Fine-Reflection-7530
selftext:
I've been experimenting with AI-assisted game development, and one thing that kept bothering me was how easily AI agents could declare a task finished when the result was still visibly wrong or the feature hadn't actually been tested.

So I started building **ForgeSkills**, an open-source collection of 20 reusable skills for AI coding agents focused on the actual game development workflow, not just generating code.

The idea is to give agents concrete procedures to follow instead of relying on vague instructions like "make it look better" or "fix the animation."

Some of what's included:

* **Reference-to-3D reconstruction:** Rebuilding assets from reference images and tracking visual differences instead of making something vaguely similar.
* **Blender automation and procedural modeling:** Creating and iterating on game-ready assets.
* **Animation and locomotion:** Addressing things like foot sliding, awkward transitions, and movement that feels wrong.
* **VFX and game feel:** Impact effects, hit stop, camera response, and coordinated feedback.
* **Gameplay engineering:** Implementing game systems with explicit requirements and validation.
* **Debugging and verification:** Reproducing issues, isolating causes, testing fixes, and checking that the result actually works.

The core workflow is:

`Measure → Build → Render → Compare → Fix → Repeat`

There are also supporting Python tools for parts of the workflow that can be measured or checked automatically.

The repository currently includes Godot and Unity pipeline skills, alongside Blender and engine-independent workflows. It's designed to work with AI coding agents that support the standard [`SKILL.md`](http://SKILL.md) format.

**GitHub:** [https://github.com/sekaikx/ForgeSkills](https://github.com/sekaikx/ForgeSkills)

It's open source under Apache-2.0.

This is still a work in progress, and I'd appreciate feedback from people who use AI agents to build actual games. I'm particularly interested in what breaks in practice, which workflows are missing, and how to make the skills more reliable with weaker models.

If you try any of them, I'd love to hear what worked and what didn't.
